A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Wolf, CapScore, and the same four core datasets. Their main text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite renumbering and layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original captioning comparisons, fine-tuning results, expert-combination and caption-length analyses, and implementation speed measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds human evaluation, alternative-judge comparisons, QA benchmark results, and an additional expert ablation.

M1.justification: The Wolf captioning procedure retains sequential image captioning, motion captions, video experts, and final LLM summarization. Object-location-to-motion summarization already appears in v1 Figure 1; v2 explains this branch and renames chain-of-thought summarization as cascading visual summarization rather than introducing a new component.

E1.justification: Section 5.4.2 adds evaluation on ActivityNet and MSRVTT using video question-answering accuracy, substantially extending evaluation beyond caption scoring on the four retained Wolf datasets. Human evaluation reuses the existing robotics videos and does not itself expand dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The captioning comparators remain CogAgent, GPT-4V, VILA-1.5, and Gemini-Pro-1.5. v2 Figure 4 adds Llama 3.2-based CapScore as a comparator to GPT-4-based CapScore against human ratings. Although other captioning metrics are discussed, their claimed appendix comparison is absent from the supplied PDF.

E3.justification: New protocols include ten human evaluators scoring 100 robotics videos, a 0–5 CapScore range test, Llama temperature tests, and VILA-1.5-13B evaluation using QA accuracy. Existing captioning and driving fine-tuning settings are retained. The stated NOTON annotation criterion also changes, without establishing that existing captions were regenerated.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands validation of CapScore through human agreement, alternative-judge and temperature checks, and score-range sensitivity. Table 6 also adds a video-only expert combination to test the contribution of the image-caption branch. The original caption-length analysis and existing expert ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix A.2 explicitly states that all experiments were run three times and averaged. v2 removes that statement, describes CapScore checks over three or '1–3' runs with variation below 0.05, and newly reports Pearson correlations with human scores. This changes statistical reporting without establishing an increase in runs or adding confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Original benchmark scores and driving fine-tuning results remain unchanged. New results include human–CapScore correlations of 0.93 and 0.95, video-only ablation scores of 0.40 similarity and 0.42 quality, and default versus fine-tuned 13B QA accuracies of 54.7 versus 55.2 on ActivityNet and 60.2 versus 60.9 on MSRVTT. Alternative-judge scores and the 0–5 scoring experiment add further findings.

T1.justification: Section 4.1.1 revises the defined NOTON lane relation: v1 describes an agent outside drivable lanes, whereas v2 describes an agent whose lane cannot directly reach the ego vehicle's lane. This is a limited categorical-definition change; the homotopy categories remain unchanged, and no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The framework, dataset, and leaderboard contributions and the abstract's performance claims remain substantially unchanged. v2 strengthens the CapScore contribution by claiming human alignment and greater effectiveness than widely used captioning metrics. It also removes the conclusion's assertion that the leaderboard guarantees data alignment.

C2.justification: Finding 2 newly attributes weak driving and robotics performance to insufficient domain training data and argues that combining experts compensates for this. v2 also interprets human correlations and range tests as evidence of CapScore reliability, and larger score gaps as greater metric effectiveness. Existing efficiency and safety limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the retained VILA configuration as 7B, specifies the GPT-4 model string, and explains motion-caption processing more explicitly. It removes the Frenet-frame lane-association detail and the appendix example-video identifier/link. Availability wording changes inconsistently: the introduction says resources are open-sourced, while Section 4.2.3 and Appendix E defer leaderboard release until publication.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning dense video captioning, LLM evaluation including CLAIR, BLEU/ROUGE, Llama, ActivityNet/MSRVTT, and Wan. These broaden contextual support, but the related-work narrative and positioning of Wolf as a combination of complementary captioning experts remain largely intact.

P1.justification: The title and author list change, terminology is revised, and dataset-curation prose is rewritten as explicit steps. New evaluation subsections and numbered findings are inserted, while appendices A.1–A.5 become A–E. Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v2 switches to a two-column layout, substantially redraws Figure 1, adds the human-evaluation figure and dataset/QA tables, and expands the ablation table. v1's fine-tuning bar chart becomes v2 Table 4 with identical values. Retained qualitative figures and the unchanged caption-length plot are resized or redistributed.

improvement.justification: Human validation, QA accuracy on additional benchmarks, and the video-only control partly address v1's dependence on its own unvalidated metric and strengthen the empirical case. The gain is limited: the reported human correlations concern five model-level scores, the advertised comparison with other captioning metrics is absent, and repeated-run averaging and the new QA protocols are insufficiently documented.
